entries.answer: I'm a Bay Area product designer focused on thoughtful interaction, clear visual systems, and responsive UI. I also like getting into the actual build when it helps, so a lot of my work mixes product thinking with hands-on HTML, CSS, and JavaScript prototyping.

I'd probably start with Funfetti if you want to see my end-to-end UX thinking. It goes from the site audit into a booking-focused user flow, stakeholder feedback, and the final responsive direction. After that, Open Source San Jose is a good follow-up for information architecture and civic-tech accessibility.

The first Funfetti direction fixed a lot of the structure, but honestly it still felt too restrained for the business. The feedback was asking for more color and energy, so I moved toward a brighter illustration-led system without losing the service and quote path.

I treated the Funfetti homepage like a decision path: explain what the business does, separate the service categories, build trust with real event imagery, and make the quote request easy to find. The final direction also includes clearer service discovery and a guided planning estimator.

The project ended with a redesigned homepage and contact path, a clearer service structure, and a more energetic visual direction. I don't have measured conversion gains or formal usability-test results for it, so I don't want to pretend those outcomes exist.

For Open Source San Jose, I reorganized the homepage around the mission, community impact, programs, and clearer ways to get involved. The main thing I was trying to improve was discovery—making the hierarchy, navigation, projects, and volunteer paths easier to understand across desktop and mobile.

entries.answer: I treated accessibility as part of the responsive product work, not a separate checklist at the end. That shows up in the hierarchy, readable content, keyboard and focus states, and the way I reviewed layouts across desktop and mobile. I wouldn't call it a formal accessibility certification, though—the portfolio shows the design decisions I made.

I use AI as a prototyping and implementation partner. I direct Codex, review the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript it produces, and test the responsive behavior myself. I think it's useful for moving faster, but I'm still responsible for the product decisions and the final quality.

For BizzNEST, I designed an edit mode where someone can change their profile content, colors, links, and layout while seeing the result in place. I also worked through reorderable content, responsive grid and list layouts, accessible states, and browser QA.

Honestly, no—not through formal user research or usability testing. I also don't have outcome metrics for it. I call that out in the project because I don't want the portfolio to make the work sound more validated than it actually is.
My resume lists a B.A. in Biology from UC Merced, which I completed in May 2025 with a 3.7 GPA. It also lists a B.S. in Computer Science from Western Governors University dated January 2026.

My resume includes work as an IT Asset Management Coordinator at ComputerCare and as a Product Innovation Extern with BeReal. So the experience is kind of a mix: operational systems and troubleshooting on one side, then competitive analysis, journey mapping, prototyping, and iterative feedback on the product side.

The main tools on my resume are Figma, GitHub, Jira, Google Workspace, Microsoft Office, NetSuite, ShipJunction, and FedEx Ship Manager. I also work with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, especially for prototyping, browser debugging, responsive layout review, and interaction details.

I like using the browser as a material and seeing what happens when the interaction itself becomes the project. Rainbow Lab explores square-based color palettes, Ink Symbiote is a pointer-reactive liquid ink field, and Hourglass Poster plays with falling sand, grain, and shifting mass.

The Music page is basically a snapshot of what I'm listening to. It includes a recent top-tracks board with Spotify links, but that data can refresh, so the page itself is the best place to check the current list.

I wanted the portfolio to feel mostly monochrome without feeling flat. It uses Space Grotesk for the main interface type and DM Mono for the smaller metadata, then brings in the off-white paper texture, black ink, thin dividers, square geometry, and restrained motion. Most of the color stays inside the project imagery so it actually means something when it shows up.
